paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yiwu in Yunnan, made in 2004, which has rested since in Guangzhou’s tea trade. Its leaf was fried in a wok and dried in the sun but never [hot-air dried](sheng:making), so some of its own activity survived, and that is what lets a cake like this keep changing. Without shou’s fermenting pile, raw pu’er [changes slowly in storage](sheng:aging) instead, and because [heat and humidity](sheng:storage) set the pace, where a cake has been kept belongs to its history.

At twenty-two years it has passed the twenty that many in the trade wait for before they call raw pu’er [aged](sheng:ageing), though some count from ten. How far it has come depends as much on that storage as on the years.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
